title: The nine goals and the thirteen weeks

story: It is Friday, 16 October, the third week of the quarter. In standup, a product manager shows RH-1234 on the screen, the small ticket that adds a "No projects yet" card to the empty projects table. "This one is tiny. Can Nova do it next week?" Nova is our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, and everyone looks at you, because you are the one learning how it is built.

Yes and no are both guesses unless you know what Nova needs before it can take a ticket, and in which week each of those things gets built. The plan has the answer, but it is 242 tickets in nine lists, and reading them from top to bottom tells you everything except the order.
hook.question: In what order is the platform built, and how do I tell when something like "Nova takes RH-1234" becomes possible?

p: The plan for this quarter is split into nine goals, called G0 to G8. Each goal is a list of tickets, and every ticket carries three planning facts: the team that owns it, its size in days (from half a day to three), and the weeks it runs in. Week 1 (W1) starts on Thursday 1 October 2026, and week 13 ends on 30 December, so W9, for example, is 26 November to 2 December.

Nine lists are hard to hold in your head, so it helps to see them as three layers plus the goals that feed them. The walls come first: G0, Guardrails and identity, builds the rules that hold even when an agent is fooled. Then the machine room: G3, Agent runtime, builds everything a run needs, such as the fresh machines, the broker and the workflow. Then the agents: G4 is Nova's pilot, and G5 is the routines, which are Nova with a different trigger and a written charter, such as a fixer for a red main branch. The other five goals feed these three. G1 measures cost and quality, and G2 does the same for Byte, our review agent. G7 makes the product's tests fast and honest, so an agent can prove its work. G6 and G8 give people and agents the same knowledge, as brain pages and as skills.
The picture below counts, for every goal and week, how many tickets are planned. You will print it yourself in the lab.

notes.text: The walls are front-loaded: most of G0 is done by week 3, with two checks for agent PRs in weeks 5 and 6.
The biggest goal: 42 tickets and 60 days, busy from week 3 to week 8, and finished with failure drills in week 9.
Nova's own goal starts only in week 6, when the runtime has its first working pieces.
Routines start small in week 3 with work that needs no agent, and run until week 12.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why week 13 is empty
p: No ticket is planned in week 13, 24 to 30 December. It is the holiday week, and it is also the only buffer in the quarter: work that slips lands there instead of moving the whole plan. In total the 242 tickets add up to 287 days of work.

read.h: Walls first, and why the order is fixed
p: The order is not a matter of taste. Here is one example. In the product repo, the backend's CI runs on every push to any branch, and it runs with CI's own credentials, which today can do far more than CI needs. The day an agent can push a branch, it can make that CI run code with those credentials. So a small ticket in week 2 narrows what CI's credentials may do, weeks before any agent can push anything.

The other walls you met in the previous lesson have the same reason to come early. The agents' own GitHub App (their identity on GitHub, with no power to merge), the LLM gateway that keeps the Anthropic key away from the machines, and the check that stops the requester from approving their own agent's work are all built in weeks 1 to 3. An agent that runs before its walls exist is exactly the accident the walls are there to prevent. That is why, when a wall ticket is late, the pilot date moves; nobody disables a wall to keep a date.

Two more rules shape the plan. First, measure before people depend on something: Nova gets TICKET-BENCH, a fixed set of past product tickets with hidden tests, so it has a score before anyone gives it real work, and Byte gets a similar gold set for its reviews. Second, work that needs no agent starts early, so every team is busy from week 1: the brain's first pages, the backend's fast test layer, Renovate for dependency updates, and a developer survey that tells us where we start from.

Now the question from standup. The ticket that hands the first product tickets to Nova is called "Start the fcp pilot". Like every ticket it has two fields about order. deps lists the tickets in its own goal that must be done first. needs is free text about what it needs from other goals, written in words such as "G7 verify commands", so a person can read it but a script can only search it.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what the chain tells you
p: Followed all the way back, the two deps become 21 tickets of Nova's goal, from week 6 to week 9: the hand-off from Jira and Slack, the readiness check, the plan and its approval buttons, the checks that are written before the code, the self-review, Byte's review of the draft, and the ready gate. Their needs name six other goals. Before the product gets Nova at all, Nova first works on tickets of its own platform repo in weeks 8 and 9, and the runtime's last ticket, a set of failure drills run with Security, lands in week 9 too.

So the honest answer in standup is: not next week. The pilot starts in weeks 9 and 10 with five to ten small tickets that the guilds choose: small frontend bugs, missing tests, small backend fixes. RH-1234 is exactly that kind of ticket, so put it on the pilot list for early December.

Seven teams own tickets, and their load is very uneven. The platform team, which builds the agent platform itself, owns most of it. DevOps owns the cloud account, the network, the machines and the deployments, and a large part of the fast test work. The backend engineers build the product's fast API test layer. Shai owns the R&D brain (reviewed pages about our systems that people and agents can search) and the trainings. Security makes the decisions about data and access and reviews the runtime before the pilot. Nave, who maintains Byte and FCP Lab (the whole product running on one machine with fake data) today, hands both over in the first weeks.

The guilds, the frontend and backend engineers, own fewer tickets, but they arrive at fixed moments, so it is worth knowing them if you are in one. In weeks 3 to 5 the guilds label real past bugs so Byte's reviews can be measured. In weeks 5 to 7 they check the brain pages about their area, write the codebase skills that teach agents their part of the product, and the frontend gets an npm run verify command. From week 9 a guild reviewer reads every Nova pull request once a week, and in weeks 10 and 11 they help build the bug fixers for their side.

p: Twelve tickets carry a flag. Three are marked decide: a choice with an owner, usually a meeting and a written decision with no code, which other tickets wait for. Nine are marked stretch: useful work we do only if there is time left, such as running two or three attempts of a hard ticket and letting the tests pick one. Every other ticket is planned work.

lab.title: Print the quarter and follow a chain
lab.goal: Turn the 242 ticket files into a timeline of the quarter, and write a script that answers "what must be done before this ticket?"

guess.q: The pilot ticket lists two tickets in its deps. Following deps back as far as they go, how many tickets of Nova's own goal must be done before the pilot can start?

options.text: 2, the two tickets in its deps list.
options.why: Those two have deps of their own, and so do theirs. You have to keep following until nothing new appears.

options.text: About 20: most of Nova's goal before week 9.
options.why: The chain grows to 21 tickets, from week 6 to week 9. Almost everything in the goal sits in front of the pilot.

options.text: All 242, because everything in the plan comes before the pilot.
options.why: deps only point inside one goal. Other goals appear in the needs text, which you read but cannot follow automatically.

lab.build: Write chain.mjs. Given part of a ticket's title on the command line, it finds that ticket, follows its deps list, then the deps of those tickets, and so on until nothing new appears. It prints every ticket it found, one line each, sorted by start week, and a last line that says how many tickets it found and which goals (G0 to G8) are named in the needs text of all of them. Run it as node chain.mjs "Start the fcp pilot", then for the runtime's last ticket, node chain.mjs "Run every failure drill", and finally for one wall, node chain.mjs "Narrow Vault".
checks: node chain.mjs "Start the fcp pilot" prints 21 tickets: the first starts in W6 and the last ones in W9.
Its last line names the goals G0 G2 G3 G6 G7 G8.
node chain.mjs "Run every failure drill" prints 32 tickets, starting in W2 with the new repo, the AWS account and the private network.
A ticket appears only once, even when two tickets in the chain depend on it.
node chain.mjs "Narrow Vault" finds 0 tickets in front of it, which is why that wall can be done in week 2.
lab.fix: A teammate's chain script says the pilot waits for only 2 tickets, so they told the product manager the pilot could start as soon as those two are done. Their code reads the deps of the pilot ticket and prints them, but never looks at the deps of those deps. Find the place where the walk must repeat, and explain how much of the plan their version hides.
explain: Why do the walls come first? Use the CI credentials example: what could go wrong if an agent could push a branch before they were narrowed?
What is the difference between deps and needs, and why can a script follow one but only search the other?
Your manager asks whether Nova can take RH-1234 next week. Using your chain output, what do you answer, and when could it happen?
lab.done: timeline.mjs draws the nine goals across 13 weeks, and chain.mjs tells you what must come before any ticket you name.

check.q: The runtime goal is two weeks late. Someone suggests turning off the check that stops requesters approving their own agent's PR, just for the first two weeks of the pilot, so it can start on time. What does the plan say?

options.text: That is fine for two weeks, as long as a senior engineer reads every agent PR.
options.why: The wall exists because people miss things under pressure. A wall that is paused when we are late is only guidance.

options.text: The pilot date moves. A wall is never disabled to keep a date.
options.why: The order is walls first, then the runtime, then the agents. If a wall or the runtime is late, everything after it moves.

options.text: Start the pilot only on frontend tickets, which do not need that check.
options.why: Every agent PR needs one approval from someone other than the requester, whatever part of the product it touches.

check.q: Which of these could start in week 1 or 2, before any agent runs?

options.text: The routine that fixes a red main branch.
options.why: A routine is Nova with another trigger. It needs the whole runtime and Nova's harness, so it comes much later.

options.text: Approve, Change and Stop buttons for Nova's plan in Slack.
options.why: Those buttons send signals to Nova's workflow, which only exists from week 6 or 7.

options.text: Writing the first pages of the R&D brain.
options.why: Pages need no agent at all. Work like this starts early on purpose, so every team is busy from week 1.

check.q: In week 3, a product manager asks whether Nova can take RH-1234 next week. What is the honest answer?

options.text: Not yet: the pilot starts in weeks 9 and 10, and RH-1234 is a good ticket for its first list.
options.why: The pilot sits at the end of a chain of 21 tickets in Nova's goal, plus the runtime and the walls. Small frontend bugs are exactly what the pilot starts with.

options.text: Yes, because the ticket is small and Nova only needs a few minutes for it.
options.why: The size of the ticket does not matter while the hand-off, the machines and the walls Nova needs do not exist yet.

options.text: Never, because the pilot only takes backend tickets.
options.why: The pilot starts with small frontend bugs, missing tests and small backend fixes, chosen with both guilds.

p: Each goal is one walkthrough part of this course, and its tickets are taught there in build order. The tickets below mark the order this lesson is about: the first ticket of the quarter, the wall that must land before any agent pushes, the runtime's final proof, and the start of the pilot.
The trust ladder of the routines repeats the same idea at a smaller scale: a routine first works in shadow mode, then sends drafts to its owner, and only then works normally.

tickets.why: The review rules are agreed and written down first; every later wall enforces them.
Narrows what CI's credentials can do, weeks before agents can push branches.
The failure drills with Security in week 9: the proof that the runtime is ready.
The start of the pilot on fcp, the end of the chain you follow in the lab.
The trust ladder: shadow, then drafts to the owner, then normal.

words.plain: One of the nine parts of the plan, G0 to G8. Each is a list of tickets with owners, days and weeks.
The thirteen weeks of the quarter. W1 starts on 1 October 2026; W13 ends on 30 December.
The tickets in the same goal that must be done first. A script can follow them.
Free text naming what a ticket needs from other goals. People read it; scripts can only search it.
A fixed set of past product tickets with hidden tests, used to score Nova before and during the pilot.
Nova's first real product tickets, from weeks 9 and 10: five to ten small ones chosen with the guilds.

review.q: From memory, put the layers in build order and name one ticket in each: walls, runtime, agents.
review.a: Walls (G0): the agents' GitHub App, the gateway, the independent-approval check, narrowing CI's credentials. Runtime (G3): the account and network, machines, broker, harness, the ticketToPr workflow, the failure drills. Agents (G4, G5): Nova's pilot and the routines.

review.q: Write the core of chain.mjs again: the function that follows deps until nothing new appears.
review.a: A recursive walk with a seen set: for each dep of the key, skip it if seen, otherwise add it and walk its deps; return the set.

review.q: A teammate says the pilot could start in week 6 if the platform team worked weekends. What is missing from that idea?
review.a: The chain in front of the pilot is not only platform work: it waits on the runtime, on DevOps machines, on the walls and on Security's review and drills, and needs from six other goals.

remember: Walls first, then the runtime, then the agents: to know when something becomes possible, follow its chain of tickets backwards.
